proposals.relationship: Cites Lévi-Strauss while arguing for a historical anthropology of mass movements, as Burke identifies.
proposals.evidence_note: Burke’s2021 discussion868/n14 explicitly identifies Mosse’s1969 review article as citing Franz Boas and Lévi-Strauss in its argument. This is a bounded named scholarly account of an anthropological resource, not a claim of direct training, complete structuralism or an independently read original article. Boas retains credit; exact Lévi-Strauss title is not invented.

proposals.relationship: Disagrees with the invention-of-tradition approach despite sharing its interest in national ritual, as Burke reports through Moro.
proposals.evidence_note: Burke869 expressly reports Mosse’s disagreement and cites Renato Moro’s2014 chapter131–136 in note20. This two-stage scholarly mediation is explicit; original Mosse statement and Moro chapter unread. Hobsbawm’s coeditor Terence Ranger retains credit, and lack of autobiography references is not treated as proof of hostility or an intellectual debt. No general rejection of every Hobsbawm work.

proposals.relationship: Questions Mosse’s emphasis on festivals and broad trends by contrasting it with attention to everyday practice, particular events and varied audience meanings.
proposals.evidence_note: Burke’s own874–875 identifies two differences and asks what a more detailed performance approach could add, while also asking later ethnographers to learn from Mosse’s broad analysis. The criticism is qualified and retrospective: it does not claim those later writers directly refuted Mosse or that he could have read work published after his death. Original monographs remain unread here.

proposals.relationship: Provides Burke with a central account of secular liturgy and political symbolism for reassessing the history of cultural and performance approaches.
proposals.evidence_note: Burke865/868 takes Nationalization of the Masses as a specific reference point for studying ritual and later performance, and876–877 credits its transformation of modern political history. This is analytical use in Burke’s own historiographical argument, not merely a publisher’s praise, formal mentoring or agreement with all Mosse conclusions. Burke’s qualification is separately represented.

proposals.relationship: Burke places Mosse alongside new cultural historians in their converging attention to ritual, representation, memory, gender and the body.
proposals.evidence_note: Burke865 explicitly describes different starting points and later converging interests, naming Davis, Thomas Laqueur and Hunt. This attributed comparison establishes no teacher-pupil relation or direction of influence. Thomas Laqueur retains credit despite lacking a graph endpoint; he is not Walter Laqueur. Original works of the compared historians remain unread for this dossier.
